outline.chapter_title: Case Background: The Social Media 'Pump and Dump' Scheme
outline.description: This chapter introduces the facts of the case, describing the defendants' actions, the specific nature of the 'pump and dump' allegations, and the initial procedural history leading to the district court's dismissal.
subtopics: Profiles of the defendants as social media influencers
Mechanics of the 'pump and dump' scheme: purchasing, pumping, and dumping
The government's allegations: material misrepresentations and illicit profits
The district court's dismissal based on the lack of a 'traditional property interest'
The government's appeal to the Fifth Circuit

outline.chapter_title: Procedural Framework: Reviewing the Sufficiency of an Indictment
outline.description: This chapter outlines the standards of review the appellate court applies when determining whether a criminal indictment sufficiently states an offense.
subtopics: The 'de novo' standard of review for indictments
The 'take as true' rule: evaluating allegations without weighing evidence
The three primary requirements for a sufficient indictment
The requirement to allege each material element of the charged offense

outline.chapter_title: Statutory Framework: Elements of Securities Fraud
outline.description: This chapter explores the specific statutes involved and the foundational legal elements required to establish securities fraud under federal law.
subtopics: Overview of 18 U.S.C. §§ 1348 and 2 (Securities Fraud)
Parallels between securities fraud and mail/wire fraud statutes
Defining the 'scheme to defraud': material misrepresentations and obtaining value
Defining 'intent to defraud': the requirements of deception and resulting harm
The distinction between 'deception' and 'obtaining money or property' as the object of fraud

outline.chapter_title: Legal Theory: Fraudulent Inducement vs. Right-to-Control
outline.description: This chapter analyzes the critical distinction between the 'right-to-control' theory (rejected by the Supreme Court) and the 'fraudulent-inducement' theory (applied by the court in this case).
subtopics: The Supreme Court's decision in Ciminelli: rejecting the right-to-control theory
What constitutes a 'traditional property interest' in federal fraud law
The fraudulent-inducement theory: tricking victims into contracts/transactions
Why the 'pump and dump' indictment constitutes fraudulent inducement
Distinguishing the deprivation of information from the deprivation of property

outline.chapter_title: The Harm Requirement: Intent and Economic Loss
outline.description: This chapter addresses the defendants' argument that the absence of a net economic loss for the victims precludes a fraud conviction, relying on the court's interpretation of recent Supreme Court precedent.
subtopics: The Supreme Court's decision in Kousisis: the absence of a net loss requirement
Distinguishing 'obtaining' property from 'harming' a victim's bottom line
The 'mirror-image' requirement: why a defendant's gain does not need to equal a victim's loss
Analyzing 'profit' as evidence of the intent to defraud
Why the receipt of market-value securities by followers does not obviate fraud charges

outline.description: This chapter summarizes the court's final ruling and its implications for prosecuting securities fraud in the age of social media influence.
subtopics: The court's reversal of the district court's dismissal
The remand for further proceedings
The confirmation of the fraudulent-inducement theory in influencer cases
Summary of the requirements for a sufficient securities fraud indictment
